businessType: Nine companion-animal general-practice veterinary clinics across one metro and two suburban counties, consolidated 16 months ago under a regional veterinary management company. 14 veterinarians, 96 total staff. ~$31M revenue TTM. The two flagship clinics were founded by a now-retired veterinarian with a 25-year local following; corporate standardized scheduling, pricing, protocols, and a preventive-care plan after acquisition.
stage: Revenue $31M TTM, up 6% YoY — but that growth is entirely price-led: average transaction value (ATV) rose 14% while total patient visits fell 7% and active patients (seen in trailing 12 months) declined from 38,400 to 34,900 (-9%). Client retention (clients returning within 18 months) fell from 79% to 68%. EBITDA margin 17% (down from 21% at acquisition; deleveraging on lower visit volume). New-client acquisition flat.
ownerGoal: Stabilize active-patient count above 36,000 and restore client retention to 75%+ within 12 months to protect the recurring-revenue base before the management company's next financing review.
ownerConstraints: Active patients fell 9% (38,400 to 34,900) and the decline is accelerating quarter over quarter; recurring wellness revenue depends on the active base.
Two flagship clinics (45% of group revenue) lost their founding veterinarian and 3 of 6 senior associate vets within 12 months of acquisition; new hires are still building client trust.
Corporate standardization raised prices 14% and changed appointment length/scheduling (shorter slots, online-only booking), drawing client complaints about access and continuity of care.
Two new corporate-backed competitor clinics and a national telehealth/vet-membership entrant opened within 5 miles of the flagship clinics in the last year.
Online review ratings at the two flagship clinics fell from 4.7 to 4.1 stars post-acquisition, with recurring themes of 'rushed visits,' 'can't see my vet,' and 'too expensive now.'
Management company financing review in 9 months expects the recurring active-patient base to be stabilizing, not eroding.
immediateConcern: Revenue is up 6% but it is masking a 9% decline in active patients and an 11-point drop in client retention (79% to 68%). The management company cannot tell whether clients are leaving because of price, because of the loss of the founding veterinarian and care-continuity changes, or because of new competition. With the active base eroding and a financing review in 9 months, leadership must decide whether to roll back pricing, invest in veterinarian recruiting/retention, or launch a client-winback program — without knowing which lever actually drives the attrition.
